organism: Rotavirus, a double-stranded RNA virus in the family Reoviridae, named for its wheel-like appearance under electron microscopy (rota is Latin for wheel). Three concentric protein shells enclose 11 gene segments; the outer shell's VP7 (G-protein) and VP4 (P-protein) define the strain's genotype and induce the neutralizing antibodies believed central to immune protection. From 1996-2005, five genotypes accounted for 90% of US strains in children under 5, with G1P[8] alone responsible for more than 75%; more recently G12P[8] has become the most common US genotype. The virus is very stable and can remain viable in the environment for weeks or months without disinfection.
clinicalFeaturesSummary: Incubation is short, usually under 48 hours. Presentation ranges from asymptomatic to severe dehydrating diarrhea with fever and vomiting - up to a third of infected children run a temperature over 39C (102F). The first infection after 3 months of age is generally the most severe; symptoms typically resolve in 3-7 days. Infants under 3 months have relatively low infection rates, likely due to passive maternal antibody and possibly breastfeeding; infection in adults is usually asymptomatic. Because clinical features and stool characteristics are nonspecific and overlap with other causes of gastroenteritis, laboratory testing is required to confirm rotavirus as the cause. Severe cases can lead to dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, and metabolic acidosis; immunocompromised children (congenital immunodeficiency, bone marrow or solid organ transplant) can develop more severe or prolonged illness with multi-organ involvement, particularly kidney and liver.
epidemiologySummary: The reservoir is the human GI tract and stool of infected people; animal rotavirus strains are antigenically distinct and rarely infect humans. Transmission is fecal-oral, through close person-to-person contact and contaminated fomites (toys, surfaces) - waterborne and foodborne spread appear uncommon. In temperate climates, disease is more common in fall and winter; in the US prevaccine era, annual epidemics progressed geographically from the Southwest (November-December) to the Northeast (April-May), a pattern that has become less distinct since vaccine introduction, replaced by a biennial activity pattern. The virus is highly communicable - nearly universal infection by age 5 in the prevaccine era - with shedding starting 2 days before diarrhea onset and continuing for several days after (over 30 days in immunocompromised people).
secularTrendsSummary: In the prevaccine era, the US saw an estimated 2.7 million infections annually, with 95% of children infected by age 5; rotavirus caused 410,000 physician visits, 200,000+ ED visits, 55,000-70,000 hospitalizations, and 20-60 deaths each year in children under 5, accounting for 30%-50% of all pediatric gastroenteritis hospitalizations. Since vaccine introduction in 2006, an evaluation of insured children estimated 280,000 clinic visits, 62,000 ED visits, and 45,000 hospitalizations averted annually (2007-2011), with documented indirect protection extending to unvaccinated children and some adults - underscoring infants' central role in driving community transmission. Vaccination coverage still lags other infant vaccines, largely because of the series' narrow age windows: only 73.6% of children born 2015-2016 completed the series by the maximum allowed age of 8 months.
vaccineDescription: An earlier vaccine (RRV-TV, Rotashield, 1998) was withdrawn within a year after postmarketing surveillance linked it to intussusception (estimated 1 excess case per 10,000 recipients). Two live oral vaccines are currently licensed: RV5 (RotaTeq, 2006), containing five human-bovine reassortant strains, and RV1 (Rotarix, 2008), containing one live attenuated human strain. Both are given orally with no adjuvant, antibiotic, or preservative; RV1's oral applicator contains latex rubber (RV5's dosing tube does not).
vaccinationScheduleSummary: RV1 is a 2-dose series (2 and 4 months); RV5 is a 3-dose series (2, 4, and 6 months); both may start as early as 6 weeks, with a minimum 4-week interval between doses. ACIP sets stricter age limits than the manufacturers' labels: the first dose must be given by 14 weeks 6 days of age, and NO dose of either vaccine should be given after 8 months 0 days of age (an off-label restriction, since RV1's label allows up to 24 weeks and RV5's up to 32 weeks) - these are hard cutoffs, not just preferred windows. If the brand used for any earlier dose is unknown, or if any dose was RV5, the child should receive a total of 3 doses to complete the series. Preterm infants can be vaccinated on the same schedule as full-term infants if chronologically at least 6 weeks old, clinically stable, and vaccinated at or after NICU/nursery discharge.
vaccineEfficacySummary: RV5's 3-dose series showed 74% efficacy against any G1-G4 rotavirus gastroenteritis and 98% against severe disease in trials, translating to real-world reductions of 86% in office visits, 94% in ED visits, and 96% in hospitalizations for that outcome. RV1's 2-dose series showed 85%-96% efficacy against severe disease depending on the trial population, and 96% efficacy against hospitalization through the second season. A meta-analysis of US case-control studies found combined ED-visit-or-hospitalization effectiveness of 84% for RV5 and 83% for RV1, with both vaccines showing broad effectiveness across genotypes. Exact duration of immunity isn't precisely known, though good efficacy has been shown through the first 2-3 years of life in the US; effectiveness in the second year of life has generally been lower than the first in lower-income countries.
contraindicationsSummary: A severe allergic reaction to a vaccine component or a prior dose is a contraindication, as is a history of intussusception (added after postmarketing studies of the current vaccines found an elevated risk - see Intussusception Risk) and severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), added after reports of vaccine-acquired rotavirus infection in SCID infants; children with known or suspected immune deficiency should be discussed with an immunologist or infectious disease specialist before vaccination. Severe latex allergy is a specific contraindication to RV1 given its latex applicator (RV5's applicator is latex-free); some experts prefer RV5 over RV1 for infants with spina bifida or bladder exstrophy, who carry elevated latex-allergy risk generally. Moderate or severe acute illness (including active gastroenteritis) is a precaution - defer until improved - though mild illness is not a reason to delay, particularly if delay would push the first dose past the 14-week-6-day cutoff. Altered immunocompetence generally is a precaution requiring individual judgment (SCID specifically is an outright contraindication); limited data haven't shown a different safety profile in HIV-infected versus uninfected infants specifically. A prior documented rotavirus infection is NOT a reason to skip vaccination - natural infection provides only partial protection, so the full series should still be completed.
vaccineSafetySummary: RV5 trials found small but statistically significant increases in diarrhea (18.1% vs 15.3% placebo) and vomiting (11.6% vs 9.9%) in the week after any dose, plus somewhat elevated rates of otitis media, nasopharyngitis, and bronchospasm over the full 42-day follow-up window; serious adverse event rates were similar to placebo. RV1 trials found elevated irritability (11.4% vs 8.7%) and flatulence (2.2% vs 1.3%) over a 31-day window, with serious adverse events again similar to placebo. Large prelicensure trials (60,000+ infants each) found no increased intussusception risk for either vaccine, but postlicensure monitoring - specifically designed to detect a risk too rare for those trials to catch - did find one (see Intussusception Risk). Occasional postmarketing detection of vaccine reassortant strains in the stool of children with diarrhea has been reported, with the reassortant virus sometimes judged the likely cause of illness.
vaccineStorageSummary: Rotavirus vaccine must be stored at refrigerator temperature, 2C to 8C (36F to 46F); manufacturer inserts include specific guidance on storing RV1's oral applicator diluent. See CDC's Vaccine Storage and Handling Toolkit for complete guidance.
surveillanceSummary: Rotavirus gastroenteritis is NOT a nationally notifiable disease in the US. Incidence and burden estimates instead come from special surveys, cohort studies, hospital discharge data review, the New Vaccine Surveillance Network, and a sentinel laboratory reporting system; CDC also runs a national strain surveillance system tracking circulating genotypes. See CDC's Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases for general reporting guidance.

supplementalTopics.title: Intussusception Risk
supplementalTopics.summary: Postlicensure evaluations of RV5 and/or RV1 in several countries, including the US, identified a low-level increased risk of intussusception (a bowel blockage where the bowel telescopes into itself) following vaccination - estimated in the US at 1 excess case per 20,000 to 100,000 vaccinated infants. The risk is concentrated in the first week after the first or second dose, though it may extend up to 21 days after the first dose. This is a much smaller risk than the earlier, withdrawn Rotashield vaccine carried (about 1 per 10,000), but it's why a personal history of intussusception is now a contraindication, and why parents and providers should know to seek prompt evaluation for any infant with possible intussusception symptoms after vaccination.

supplementalTopics.title: Vaccinating Around Immunocompromised or Pregnant Household Members
supplementalTopics.summary: Infants living with an immunocompromised person can still be vaccinated on schedule - the indirect protection the vaccinated infant provides to that household member is judged to outweigh the small risk of vaccine-virus transmission to them. The same applies to infants living with a pregnant household member: because most women of childbearing age already have pre-existing rotavirus immunity, the infection risk from vaccine virus is considered very low, though good hand hygiene after diaper changes is still sensible for the whole household.

keyPoints: Not identified as a cause of diarrhea until 1973, by electron microscopy of intestinal tissue
An earlier vaccine (Rotashield, 1998) was withdrawn within a year after being linked to intussusception - the current vaccines carry a much smaller version of that same risk
ACIP sets stricter, off-label age cutoffs than either manufacturer's own label: no first dose after 14 weeks 6 days, and no dose of any kind after 8 months 0 days
A documented prior rotavirus infection does not exempt an infant from completing the vaccine series - natural infection gives only partial protection
Rotavirus vaccination has shown indirect (herd) protection benefits to unvaccinated children and even some adults, highlighting infants' outsized role in community transmission
Rotavirus gastroenteritis is not a nationally notifiable disease in the US, unlike most other diseases in this library
US vaccination coverage lags other infant vaccines largely because of the unusually narrow, hard-cutoff dosing age window
